title: Joan of Arc Burned: Heresy, Diabolism, and Gender Transgression
description:
Joan of Arc was burned at the stake in Rouen on 30 May 1431 following a trial conducted by the Bishop of Beauvais, Pierre Cauchon, under English political supervision. The charges against her included heresy, idolatry, and relapse into heresy, with particular emphasis on her refusal to wear women's clothing, her claim to receive direct divine revelation, and her insistence on the authority of her 'voices' against the authority of the Church. Joan's trial was not technically a witchcraft trial — she was not charged with maleficium or diabolical pact — but it occupied an overlapping zone between heresy procedure and the emerging witch trial, and involved extensive examination of whether her visions and voices were of divine or demonic origin.

The gender dimensions of Joan's trial are especially significant for the history of witchcraft prosecution. Her cross-dressing was treated as a sign of diabolical inversion — a woman usurping male authority in both military and spiritual domains. The boundary between a female visionary recognized as holy and one condemned as diabolically deceived was thin and politically determined. Joan's judges followed exactly the procedure that contemporary theologians recommended for discerning true from false spiritual experience, and they reached the theologically defensible conclusion that her voices were demonic. Her rehabilitation in 1456 explicitly reversed these findings.

The Joan of Arc case thus illustrates the intersection of gender politics, institutional ecclesiastical authority, and the developing framework of diabolical heresy that would later fuel the witch trials. The question of whether female spiritual authority was divinely inspired or demonically deceived was not rhetorical but had life-or-death stakes, as Joan's case demonstrated to all contemporaries.
historiographical_note: Régine Pernoud and Marie-Véronique Clin's Joan of Arc: Her Story (1998) provides the essential documentary account. Lyndal Roper's gender-focused witchcraft scholarship illuminates how Joan's case exemplifies the dangerous intersection of female religious authority and diabolical accusation. Anne Llewellyn Barstow connects Joan's trial explicitly to the gendered dimensions of witch prosecution.
source_method: Published trial records (fully surviving); secondary scholarship on Joan of Arc and heresy procedure
